summary: Teaches area of a rectangle with fractional side lengths as a visual demonstration of fraction multiplication: a unit square cut in two directions (e.g. thirds one way, quarters the other) forms b×d tiles each worth 1/(b×d), and shading the a×c corner block gives ac/bd of the unit. The core insight is that the unit square is REDEFINED by the two partitions — denominators multiply because there are b×d tiles per unit, numerators multiply because a×c tiles are shaded. Learners must both READ a given tiled diagram (naming one tile's value and the multiplication it shows) and PRODUCE one for a fresh product. Worked example: 2/3 × 3/4 gives 3×4=12 tiles, 2×3=6 shaded = 6/12 = 1/2 — an area smaller than either side because both sides are less than 1.
misconceptions: Reads the tile as 1/(b+d) — e.g. 1/7 for a 3-by-4 partition — adding the partitions instead of multiplying (area treated additively)
Confuses area with perimeter — measures the boundary of the shaded rectangle rather than counting interior tiles
Partitions in only one direction, so the two-dimensional tile is never formed and denominators are not multiplied
Loses the unit square: counts shaded tiles as a whole number (6) rather than 6 of 12 of ONE unit
Believes area must be larger than the sides, so distrusts an area (1/2) smaller than either side length

activities.title: Build the area and watch the tiles appear
steps: Start from one whole unit square. Partition it in two directions — cut it into 3 columns one way and 4 rows the other way — to model 2/3 × 3/4.
Count the small tiles that appear in the whole unit square (3 across × 4 down = 12) and name the value of ONE tile: 1/12 of the unit square.
Shade the 2-by-3 corner block (2 of the 3 columns, 3 of the 4 rows) and count the shaded tiles: 2×3 = 6, so 6 tiles = 6/12 = 1/2.
Compare the shaded rectangle against the whole unit square and confirm it is exactly half of it — an area smaller than either side length (because each side is less than 1).
Say aloud which number in the picture gives the denominator (3×4 = 12 tiles per unit) and which gives the numerator (2×3 = 6 shaded tiles).
activities.insight: Cutting the unit square in two directions redefines the unit into b×d equal tiles (so denominators multiply) and the shaded a×c block gives the numerator — this is why (a/b)×(c/d) = ac/bd, and why the product can be smaller than both sides when both sides are less than 1.

activities.title: Read a tiled diagram and justify each number
steps: Look at a fully tiled 2/3 × 3/4 diagram. Point to one tile and state its value, then state the multiplication the whole shaded rectangle shows.
Answer: why is one tile 1/12 and not 1/7? Trace the two-way cut that creates the grid to justify your answer.
Point to the part of the picture that gives the 12 (3 columns × 4 rows) and the part that gives the 6 (the 2×3 shaded block).
Match the diagram to its equation (a/b)×(c/d) = ac/bd, identifying the tiles that justify each factor.
activities.insight: Reading a tiled area diagram means naming the counting unit (1/(b×d)) and recognising the shaded block as the product — the two-directional grid of 3 columns × 4 rows, not adding the columns and rows (3 + 4), is what makes each tile a twelfth.

activities.title: Produce your own diagram for a fresh product
steps: On a blank unit square, DRAW a rectangle showing 1/2 × 4/5: choose the two cuts yourself — partition into 2 one way and 5 the other way.
Name what one tile is worth (1/10) and explain why: 2×5 = 10 tiles fill the unit.
Shade a 1-by-4 block (4 tiles) and read the area: 4/10 = 2/5.
Say which cuts produced the 10 and which shaded tiles produced the 4, pointing to each number in your own drawing.

Extend the model: tile across more than one unit square to find the area of a rectangle with sides 1 1/2 and 2/3 (here the product is 1, larger than the 2/3 side — a useful check that the 'smaller than both' intuition only applies when both sides are less than 1).
activities.insight: Choosing both partitions yourself — not just one — is what shows you own the idea that two cuts redefine the unit; the model scales to mixed numbers by tiling more than one unit square.

checkQuestion: Here is a rectangle drawn 2/3 of a unit wide and 3/4 of a unit tall, tiled with small equal squares. First, tell me: what fraction of one whole unit square is ONE small tile, and what multiplication does the whole shaded rectangle show? Then, on this fresh unit grid, DRAW a rectangle that shows 1/2 × 4/5, and use your drawing to find the area.
checkAnswer: One tile is 1/12 of the unit square (the unit is cut into 3 columns and 4 rows, 3×4 = 12 tiles). The shaded rectangle shows 2/3 × 3/4, covering 2×3 = 6 tiles = 6/12 = 1/2. For 1/2 × 4/5: partition the unit into 2 (one way) and 5 (the other) → 10 tiles each 1/10; shade a 1-by-4 block = 4 tiles = 4/10 = 2/5.
